questions.q: What is the difference between encryption at rest and encryption in transit?
options: They are two names for the same protection
Encryption at rest protects stored data (disk, database, backup); encryption in transit protects data while it's moving across a network
Encryption at rest only applies to asymmetric encryption; encryption in transit only applies to symmetric encryption
Encryption in transit is a Salesforce-specific feature with no general definition
questions.explain: At-rest protects stored data; in-transit protects data moving across a network (typically via TLS) -- a system can have one configured without the other, so an architect must verify both separately.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say encryption is not a substitute for an authorization control?
options: Because encryption only works on text fields, never on numbers
Because Salesforce Shield has been deprecated in favor of authorization-only controls

Because encryption protects data from someone bypassing the application entirely (e.g., a stolen disk), but does nothing to stop a legitimately authenticated, authorized user from reading the data through the normal application interface
Because authorization controls always run faster than encryption
questions.explain: Encryption protects confidentiality from someone outside the normal access path; it does nothing about a legitimately authorized user viewing the field through the application -- that's specifically what FLS, sharing, and CRUD permissions are for.

questions.q: In the lesson's key-management point, why is key management usually described as the hardest part of an encryption design?
options: Because encryption algorithms themselves are usually broken within a few years
Because key management is not actually necessary for symmetric encryption
Because keys must be changed every single time data is read
Because an encryption scheme is only as strong as the protection around its keys -- an attacker who steals the key doesn't need to break the algorithm at all
questions.explain: The math behind modern encryption algorithms is generally sound; the practical weak point is almost always how the keys themselves are generated, stored, rotated, and protected -- stealing the key bypasses the algorithm's strength entirely.

questions.q: In the Lab scenario (SSNs encrypted at rest, but FLS set to Visible for every Service Agent profile, with no monitoring), what does this lesson say the encryption actually protects against?
options: It protects against someone bypassing the application entirely, such as accessing raw storage or a stolen backup -- it does not restrict which authenticated users can see the field through the normal UI
Nothing at all -- the encryption provides zero protection in this configuration
It fully protects the data from every Service Agent viewing it
It protects against monitoring gaps specifically
questions.explain: Encryption at rest still protects against someone who gets the raw storage without going through the application -- but since FLS is wide open and nothing monitors access, the scenario has a real, unaddressed authorization and monitoring gap for legitimate-looking access.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish what encryption protects against from what monitoring protects against?
options: Encryption and monitoring protect against the exact same failure mode, so configuring one makes the other unnecessary

Encryption limits damage if data is exposed outside normal access paths; monitoring tries to detect unusual activity happening through the normal access paths, so misuse of legitimate access doesn't go unnoticed
Monitoring is a type of encryption applied to log files
Encryption only matters for data in transit; monitoring only matters for data at rest
questions.explain: The two controls address different failure modes -- encryption protects data if it's exposed outside the normal path, while monitoring watches for unusual use of legitimate, normal access -- and neither one substitutes for the other.
